Psychologists have long been interested in how we construct our identities and the sorts of strategies that we use to present ourselves in society. New findings suggest that the kinds of ___26___ and strategic self-presentation behaviour we see in adults appear at a much younger age than ___27___ known. 

Research shows that a child’s awareness of social standing comes from adults. Like grown-ups, kids want to be ___28___ by those they admire. Interactive experiences may provide opportunities for children to learn about what ___29___ a desirable reputation and the kinds of strategies that are effective for ___30___ a good reputation in their social environment. 

Five-year-olds aren’t just aware of their reputations, they also behave strategically to alter their outward image. They will ___31___ their behaviour in order to appear moral or socially good in the eyes of key observers. While we know that adults use a large variety of attributes to manage and create impressions, we don’t yet know whether children ___32___ and use the fact that different attributes are valuable at different times to different ___33___. It’s important for us to further consider where in this process children succeed in controlling their reputation and where they ___34___. 

A question to think about is, “What happens even earlier than age five?” Children don’t just show up to the first day of kindergarten and have the idea of reputation pop ___35___ into existence. The logical question to ask is, “What happens even earlier?”

paragraphs.content: Recently, a leading design federation in the UK warned that the UK could face a creative skills shortage, after the latest figures revealed a drop of almost 10 percent in students studying Design and Technology. These figures showed that the number of pupils that sat exams in Design and Technology fell 10 percent from 204,788 to 185,279 last year.

Chief executive John Kampfner of the Creative Industries Federation thinks that this drop in figures has worrying implications for the skills pipeline in Britain’s hugely successful arts and creative industries. He said, “We already have skills shortages in many jobs such as animation (动画制作) and special effects.” He added: “Engineering, which requires a similar mix of creative and technical skills, also has recruitment problems.”

Many other designers and architects have expressed concern over the future supply of home-grown talent for UK firms, and industry bodies have pointed out that there has been a lack of roots-level support. However, if these designers had visited the Design Museum shop in London earlier this year their fears may have been eased. With £10 to spend, they could have bought a fascinating children’s toy called “Dazzle Racer”. An automotive cylinder(圆柱体), it included a wind-up, elastic (有弹性的)-band-powered mechanism, minimal parts, all 100 percent recycled and lots of stickers. It was good fun, simple, eye-catching and very original.

Well you’d expect the Design Museum to commission and make some interesting items, but this one was different. Designed by a group of six Year 9 and Year 10 boys from Finchley Catholic High School, the toy was the winning entry in the museum’s 2015 Design Ventura competition, which brings the business of design to life for students aged 13 to 16 by challenging them to develop a new creative, sustainable and commercially feasible product for the Design Museum shop and attracts hundreds of entries nationwide.

“We did Design Ventura in my previous school,” says Liam Hourican, Finchley Catholic High School’s design technology curriculum leader. “Then when I changed schools four years ago, I introduced it here because it helps to develop so many skills.”

The theme for last year’s competition was “Move”, and Hourican began with three groups working in lunch breaks and after school before selecting the group with the most innovative idea. Each participating school may submit just one proposal. “It’s the taking part and doing the work which is important,” he says. “And I never dreamt we’d win.”

Catherine Ritman Smith, head of learning at the Design Museum, is expecting around 10,000 participants aged 13 to 16 to take part this year and says that the project — funded by Deutsche Bank as part of its youth engagement programme Born To Be — is the biggest event in the museum’s calendar. “We started Design Ventura with around 800 young people in 2010 and it has grown steadily since,” she says. “Teachers like it because the skills are all transferable and it helps to validate the value of design as a subject,” she explains, telling me that nearly 600 schools have taken part so far.

So how does the competition work? A single-word theme is announced in the summer. This year it is “Change”. Schools work with groups to produce imaginative design ideas for a product in simple materials that could sell for £10 in the Design Museum Shop. Participating schools then register by November and eventually submit their design idea. Along the way there is training and support for teachers and tutoring for students from designers. An additional bonus is when the winners see their design on sale in the spring of the following year.

Hourican and his pupils have happy memories of spending a whole day at the museum, having been selected as one of 10 shortlisted schools to present their idea to a panel of judges, including designer Jasper Conran. Then they worked with the Kin Design Studio in Shoreditch, met designers at their school and attended a lunch with Deutsche Bank employees. The students helped to make decisions and there were plenty of discussions — they changed the product’s name, for example.

“One of the really useful things about this competition,” says Hourican, “is that there’s a commercial element because the product is going on sale for real and the boys had to learn about budgeting and marketing, as well as designing their game.” Profits go to charity. “The winning team chooses where it wants the profits to go,” says Ritman Smith. “The Finchley Catholic High School product raised about £1,000 for Great Ormond Street Hospital.” Winning entries in past years have included a make-your-own cloth kit called Dove Bunting and a threefold, wallet-sized travel game with goals at each end, called Badoiiing.

It costs the schools nothing to participate in Design Ventura; the professional designers provide their services for free. Among them are architect Asif Khan, a Design Museum trustee who has worked as designer-in-residence at the museum, helping emerging architects. He has recently been commissioned to design the new Museum of London building in Smithfield.

Another is television presenter and interior designer Naomi Cleaver, who is one of the competition’s judges. “I'm very keen to encourage young people,” she says, observing that design brings together other subjects such as literature, art, history, geography and science. “Now that design education is limited in the curriculum, I’m all in favour of competitions such as Design Ventura, which helps to bring the standard curriculum to life,” says Cleaver. “And the judging day is terrific fun. Some of these students are very imaginative. One group presented their idea in the form of a puppet show and we see some marvelous demonstration models. “I’m always impressed by the levels of confidence and the support the students get from their teachers.”

Ritman Smith adds: “Design technology has become a tricky subject to make a case for, and we’ve heard of departments closing in some schools. We find that if pupils take part in Design Ventura in Year Nine it can be the trigger which leads them to opt for it at General Certificate of Secondary Education, so we are helping to keep alive something which is crucial to industry and entrepreneurship.”

passages.title: Passage One
passages.content:
New research suggests that pandas may be at risk of dying out because they are too comfortable. Experts say too much happiness can stop the bears from searching for new mates.

Environmentalists have long believed that building roads or homes near the bears may threaten their survival by “reducing or fragmenting their natural habitats”, The Times reported. But the new research suggests that a “modest degree of discomfort and fragmentation” may actually help preserve panda populations.

The research was conducted by scientists from Michigan State University. It concluded that pandas fail to wander off in search of new mates if they find their habitat too comfortable, resulting in a lack of vital genetic diversity.

For their study — outlined in a paper in the journal Conservation Biology — the team looked at genetic diversity and spread among a Chinese panda population. The ideal level of perfectly livable habitat was found to be only 80% of an area, with the remainder either too harsh or too affected by human activity.

The experts concluded that pandas should ideally “be happy enough to thrive, but not so content that they don’t want to move around and find new mates”.

Their conclusions about what The Guardian described as this “sweet spot” are in line with the so-called Goldilocks principle: that there can be just the right amount of something. The concept has been applied to a wide range of disciplines, from developmental psychology to economics and engineering.

Claudio Sillero, a professor of conservation biology at Oxford University, told the newspaper that the new findings could have implications beyond panda conservation.

“Most large animals that eat meat live in increasingly fragmented landscapes,” said Sillero, who was not involved in the research. “It may well be that the messy nature of their relationship with human efforts induces more animals to scatter or travel further, and might result in greater genetic connectivity and enhanced population persistence.”

The most recent count of pandas found that there were more than 1,800 left in the wild, putting them on the list of vulnerable, but not endangered, species.

passages.title: Passage Two
passages.content:
With those born with natural talents, it feels as if they excel without really trying. But what about those of us who don’t have a natural talent? We’ve been told all our lives that if you work hard, you too can succeed. But with the release of Angela Duckworth’s Grit, we are given a new key to success.

“As much as talent counts, effort counts twice,” says Duckworth in Grit. She introduces a new concept that talent may be overrated, and if you want real success, what you need is grit the perfect combination of passion and persistence. Even if you have natural talent it’s nothing without grit.

Duckworth says grit is the difference between success and failure. A person who has grit is more likely to succeed than a person who does not. When we think about attaining success — whether it’s landing that job or learning that new skill — our thoughts are immediately burdened by all the things we must first learn. If you want that new job, you have to learn the job skills, then the interview skills, then the dress part — and you must be perfect at all of them. Grit is different because it tells us that perfection isn’t the goal.

Grit lifts the unreasonable expectations off our shoulders. Grit tells us that the door is open wider than we first thought possible. Grit allows us to redefine our goals. Think about it: what’s something you’ve always wanted to do, but gave up because you “don’t have the skills for it”? What’s something you love but aren’t good at?

The real workings of grit are to have sustainable passion and continue to try. Effort means more than your natural ability. Even if you haven’t mastered a skill, grit tells you that you can still succeed if you can transform your passion into action. In a way, Duckworth is giving new hope to people who have shut the doors on their dreams. She is saying it is possible that you can accomplish anything. If at first you fail, then try one more time with grit.

00:03:35,940 --> 00:03:41,740
Jacks and Goodman each face up to five years in federal prison for the mail thefts and
杰克斯和古德曼因邮件盗窃各面临最高五年的联邦监禁，

35
00:03:41,740 --> 00:03:44,680
up to ten years for possession of the postal key.
因持有邮政钥匙各面临最高十年的监禁。

36
00:03:45,320 --> 00:03:49,700
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
问题 3 和 4 基于你刚刚听到的新闻报道。

37
00:03:50,280 --> 00:03:51,240
Question 3.
问题 3。

38
00:03:51,240 --> 00:03:56,980
What did Jordan Jacks and Tarad Goodman do according to a news release?
根据新闻发布稿，乔丹·杰克斯和塔拉德·古德曼做了什么？

39
00:04:10,940 --> 00:04:15,920
Question 4. What do Jordan Jacks and Tarad Goodman face?
问题 4。乔丹·杰克斯和塔拉德·古德曼面临什么样的处罚？

40
00:04:29,760 --> 00:04:32,000
News Report 3.
新闻报道 3。

41
00:04:32,900 --> 00:04:38,140
Can fast fashion be sustainable? Researchers think yes.
快时尚能可持续发展吗？研究人员认为是可以的。

42
00:04:38,140 --> 00:04:45,000
Identifying why the fast-fashion business model creates waste and determining whether regulators
找准快时尚商业模式产生浪费的原因，并确定监管机构

43
00:04:45,000 --> 00:04:51,460
can establish incentives for consumers and manufacturers are steps to reduce waste.
能否为消费者和制造商建立激励机制，是减少浪费的步骤。

44
00:04:52,840 --> 00:04:58,060
Recently, the clothing industry has come under attack for creating a waste problem
近来，服装行业因造成浪费问题而饱受抨击，

45
00:04:58,060 --> 00:05:05,060
with serious environmental consequences. In the absence of environmentally and economically feasible
并带来了严重的环保后果。在缺乏环保且经济可行的

46
00:05:05,060 --> 00:05:11,220
recycling options, fast-fashion manufacturers pump out low-quality clothes,
回收方案的情况下，快时尚制造商大量生产低质服装，

47
00:05:11,220 --> 00:05:16,860
produced in high volumes that are worn only a few times and then discarded.
这些衣服在穿过几次后就会被丢弃。

48
00:05:17,460 --> 00:05:26,800
The researchers put forth policy contributions ranging from sustainable disposal of leftover stock to production tax,
研究人员提出了多项政策建议，包括剩余库存的可持续处理以及征收生产税，

49
00:05:26,800 --> 00:05:32,120
to incentivize both manufacturers and consumers to be more waste conscious.
以激励制造商和消费者都更具环保意识。

50
00:05:33,040 --> 00:05:39,040
In order to devise effective policies to curb the environmental impact of the clothing industry,
为了制定有效政策来遏制服装行业对环境的影响，

51
00:05:39,040 --> 00:05:44,340
it is important to identify the source of the problem in the supply chain.
找准供应链中问题的源头至关重要。

52
00:05:45,140 --> 00:05:52,460
Manufacturers, consumers, and regulatory bodies can then take an informed approach to recognize
制造商、消费者和监管机构随后可以采取明智的方法，来认识

53
00:05:52,460 --> 00:05:55,360
the environmental impact of fast fashion,
快时尚对环境的影响，

54
00:05:56,360 --> 00:06:03,260
and to design an ecosystem to reduce waste, incentivize innovation, and create new business
并设计一个生态系统来减少浪费、激励创新，并创建新的商业模式

55
00:06:03,260 --> 00:06:05,020
models to manage waste.
来管理浪费。

56
00:06:05,940 --> 00:06:11,140
Questions 5-7 are based on the news reports you have just heard.
问题 5-7 基于你刚刚听到的新闻报道。

57
00:06:11,840 --> 00:06:12,680
Question 5.
问题 5。

58
00:06:13,460 --> 00:06:16,320
Why has the clothing industry come under attack?
服装行业为什么会受到抨击？

59
00:18:30,120 --> 00:06:36,200
Question 6. Why do the researchers put forth such policies as production tax?
问题 6。为什么研究人员提出征收生产税等政策？

60
00:06:50,620 --> 00:06:56,880
Question 7. What should be done first to eliminate the harm caused by the clothing industry?
问题 7。要消除服装行业造成的危害，首先应该做什么？

1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:16,840
Section B, directions. In this section, you will hear two long conversations. At the end of each conversation, you will hear four questions. Both the conversation and the questions will be spoken only once.
第二节，说明。在本节中，你将听到两段长对话。在每段对话结束时，你将听到四个问题。对话和问题都只播放一遍。

2
00:00:16,840 --> 00:00:25,220
After you hear a question, you must choose the best answer from the four choices, mark the A, B, C and D.
听完问题后，你必须从 A、B、C、D 四个选项中选出最佳答案。

3
00:00:26,160 --> 00:03:31,760
Then mark the corresponding letter on Answer Sheet 1 with a single line through the center.
然后在答题卡 1 上相应的字母中心划一条单线进行涂黑。

4
00:00:33,699 --> 00:00:34,980
Conversation 1.
对话 1。

5
00:00:35,340 --> 00:00:38,920
Hey Mary, you seem to be very much annoyed. What happened?
嘿，玛丽，你看起来很烦躁。发生什么事了？

6
00:00:39,700 --> 00:00:42,320
Rush Hour in this city is killing me.
这个城市的早晚高峰简直要了我的命。

7
00:00:42,320 --> 00:00:47,880
I, yes, Rush Hour is terrible, especially in the morning between 8 and 9.
唉，是的，高峰期确实很可怕，尤其是早上 8 点到 9 点之间。

8
00:00:48,460 --> 00:00:51,140
But what else can you expect in a city this big?
但在这么大的城市里，你还能指望什么呢？

9
00:00:51,780 --> 00:00:55,100
Well, I think the local government could help improve things.
嗯，我觉得当地政府可以帮忙改善现状。

10
00:00:55,420 --> 00:01:01,500
I mean, getting rid of Rush Hour maybe impossible, but it could be made more tolerable.
我的意思是，消除高峰期可能不现实，但可以让它变得更易于忍受。

11
00:01:01,800 --> 00:01:02,620
Don't you think?
你不觉得吗？

12
00:01:03,160 --> 00:01:06,100
Um, but I'm not sure how.
嗯，但我不知道该怎么做。

13
00:01:06,680 --> 00:01:10,820
Well, for example, the subway system could have air conditioning.
比如，地铁系统可以加装空调。

14
00:01:10,820 --> 00:01:15,600
I know many cities in the world have air conditioning in their subway.
我知道世界上很多城市的地铁里都有空调。

15
00:01:16,240 --> 00:01:17,540
So why can't we?
为什么我们不行？

16
00:01:18,140 --> 00:01:22,520
It gets so hot in the summer I can hardly breathe down there.
夏天下面太热了，我在那儿几乎没法呼吸。

17
00:01:22,860 --> 00:01:28,560
And add to that the rush hour crowds with strangers packed close together in the subway
再加上高峰期的人潮，陌生人们在地铁车厢里
 
18
00:01:28,560 --> 00:01:29,260
carriages.
紧紧挤在一起。

19
00:01:29,960 --> 00:01:31,800
The whole thing is just horrible.
整件事简直太糟糕了。

20
00:01:32,860 --> 00:01:35,040
Ah yes, you are completely right.
啊是的，你完全正确。

21
00:01:35,580 --> 00:01:37,080
The trains here are too old.
这里的火车太旧了。

22
00:01:37,080 --> 00:01:41,200
The government should definitely invest in new ones with air conditioning.
政府绝对应该投资购买带空调的新车。

23
00:01:41,940 --> 00:01:44,740
I guess I'm fortunate I take the bus instead.
我想我很幸运，我是坐公交车的。

24
00:01:45,140 --> 00:01:46,360
Oh, that's much better.
噢，那好多了。

25
00:01:46,700 --> 00:01:48,160
Yeah, it's more convenient.
是的，更方便。

26
00:01:48,860 --> 00:01:52,340
Bus number 36 goes straight from my house to the office.
36 路公交车直接从我家开到办公室。

27
00:01:52,720 --> 00:01:56,140
It's a 30 minute ride and I don't have to make any changes.
30 分钟车程，而且不用换乘。

28
00:01:56,500 --> 00:01:57,700
That sounds nice.
听起来不错。

29
00:01:58,160 --> 00:02:01,380
I tell you, my current commute is killing me.
告诉你，我现在的通勤快把我逼疯了。

30
00:02:01,720 --> 00:02:03,920
Maybe I should move closer to the office.
也许我应该搬到离办公室近点的地方。

31
00:02:04,440 --> 00:02:06,740
Well, I know a great housing agent.
嗯，我认识一个很棒的房产中介。

32
00:02:06,740 --> 00:02:10,780
I found the flat I'm living in now through him and I love it.
我现在住的公寓就是通过他找的，我很喜欢。

33
00:03:20,000 --> 00:02:13,460
Hmm, could you send me his number please?
嗯，能把他的号码发给我吗？

34
00:02:13,660 --> 00:02:19,600
Sure thing. Just tell him exactly what you are looking for and I'm sure he will find something good.
没问题。只要告诉他你具体想要什么样的，我相信他会找到合适的。

35
00:02:20,260 --> 00:02:24,600
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
问题 8 到 11 是基于你刚刚听到的对话。

36
00:02:25,320 --> 00:02:27,940
Question 8. Why is the woman complaining?
问题 8。这位女士为什么抱怨？

37
00:02:42,340 --> 00:02:46,440
Question 9. What does the woman suggest doing?
问题 9。这位女士建议做什么？

38
00:03:00,840 --> 00:03:05,400
Question 10. What do we learn about the man from the conversation?
问题 10。从对话中我们了解到了关于这位男士的什么信息？

39
00:03:20,160 --> 00:03:30,980
Question 11. What does the woman ask the man to do at the end of the conversation?
问题 11。在对话结束时，这位女士要求男士做什么？

40
00:03:40,760 --> 00:03:41,960
Conversation 2
对话 2

41
00:03:41,960 --> 00:03:43,460
Did you hear about Johnny?
你听说了约翰尼的事吗？

42
00:03:44,160 --> 00:03:45,980
No, why? Is he okay?
没有，怎么了？他还好吗？

43
00:03:46,320 --> 00:03:48,160
He had some plastic surgery done.
他去做整形手术了。

44
00:03:48,480 --> 00:03:49,340
What? Why?
什么？为什么？

45
00:03:49,960 --> 00:03:52,620
Do you remember he had a scar on his face?
你记得他脸上有一道疤吗？

46
00:03:53,080 --> 00:03:55,420
Yes, of course. He always had that.
当然记得。他一直都有那道疤。

47
00:03:55,660 --> 00:04:00,580
I've known him since primary school, and I always remember him having that on his cheek.
我从小学就认识他了，一直记得他脸颊上有那个。

48
00:04:00,580 --> 00:04:03,080
Well, he had it fixed.
嗯，他把它修整了。

49
00:04:03,940 --> 00:04:04,340
Fixed?
修整？

50
00:04:04,360 --> 00:04:05,120
What do you mean?
你什么意思？

51
00:04:05,500 --> 00:04:07,180
You can't fix a scar.
疤痕是没法“修好”的。

52
00:04:07,840 --> 00:04:09,000
You know what I mean.
你知道我的意思。

53
00:04:09,240 --> 00:04:11,120
He had an operation done on it.
他动了个手术。

54
00:04:11,380 --> 00:04:15,120
Plastic surgery in order to cover it and make it less noticeable.
做整形手术是为了遮盖它，让它不那么明显。

55
00:04:16,160 --> 00:04:18,880
Oh, well, that's ridiculous, isn't it?
噢，好吧，这太荒谬了，不是吗？

56
00:04:19,100 --> 00:04:20,640
It was noticeable, sure.
虽然是很明显。

57
00:04:21,040 --> 00:04:22,920
But it wasn't an ugly scar.
但那并不是一道丑陋的疤。

58
00:04:23,460 --> 00:04:27,180
It never occurred to me that he should have it taken care of like that.
我从未想过他需要用那种方式去处理它。

59
00:04:27,500 --> 00:04:28,080
I agree.
我同意。

60
00:04:28,080 --> 00:04:34,080
I can understand some scars and physical defects can be ugly and distracting, but not
我可以理解有些疤痕和身体缺陷可能很丑陋且引人分心，但
 
61
00:04:34,080 --> 00:04:34,880
Johnny's.
约翰尼的那个不是。

62
00:04:35,000 --> 00:04:39,900
In fact, I thought it added character, like it gave him a certain uniqueness.
事实上，我觉得那增加了他的个性，让他有一种独特性。

63
00:04:40,920 --> 00:04:42,900
He must have felt differently though.
不过他本人的感觉肯定不一样。

64
00:04:43,080 --> 00:04:47,160
He must have felt self-conscious and insecure perhaps.
他肯定觉得很局促，甚至可能感到自卑。

65
00:04:47,580 --> 00:04:49,520
No, no, that's not the reason.
不，不，那不是原因。

66
00:04:49,920 --> 00:04:52,000
He was totally fine with his scar.
他对他那道疤完全没意见。

67
00:04:52,320 --> 00:04:55,280
As he said, he had had it for most of his life.
正如他所说，那道疤伴随了他大半辈子。

68
00:04:55,280 --> 00:04:57,600
Then why did he have the operation?
那他为什么要动手术？

69
00:04:58,120 --> 00:05:00,380
Because his girlfriend wanted him to.
因为他的女朋友想让他做。

70
00:05:00,840 --> 00:05:04,440
What? That's so superficial and selfish of her.
什么？她也太肤浅、太自私了。

71
00:05:04,620 --> 00:05:07,940
If Johnny's girlfriend doesn't like him for who he is,
如果约翰尼的女朋友不喜欢他真实的样子，

72
00:05:08,260 --> 00:05:10,580
then she does not deserve to be his girlfriend.
那她就不配当他的女朋友。

73
00:05:11,020 --> 00:05:14,840
You're right. So he is a fool to give in to her like that.
你说得对。所以他居然就这样向她妥协，真是个傻瓜。

74
00:05:15,040 --> 00:05:20,160
But when I told him, he said he loves her and would just do what she wants him to.
但当我告诉他时，他说他爱她，只想按她的意愿去做。

75
00:05:20,740 --> 00:05:22,120
What a fool he is.
他真是个傻瓜。

76
00:05:22,120 --> 00:05:31,080
Question 12-15 are based on the conversation you have just heard. Question 12. What does the man say about Johnny?
问题 12-15 是基于你刚刚听到的对话。问题 12。这位男士说了关于约翰尼的什么？

77
00:05:44,920 --> 00:05:49,020
Question 13. What does the woman find puzzling?
问题 13。这位女士觉得什么事很令人费解？

78
00:06:03,039 --> 00:06:07,560
Question 14. What did the man think of Johnny's scar?
问题 14。这位男士怎么看约翰尼的疤痕？

79
00:06:21,600 --> 00:06:27,620
Question 15. How could we describe the speakers' attitude towards Johnny's girlfriend?
问题 15。我们该如何描述说话者对约翰尼女朋友的态度？

1

Section C, directions, in this section you will hear three passages.
第三节，说明。在本节中，你将听到三篇短文。

2
00:00:08,880 --> 00:00:12,900
At the end of each passage, you will hear three or four questions.
在每篇短文结束时，你将听到三到四个问题。

3
00:00:13,920 --> 00:00:17,900
Both the passage and the questions will be spoken only once.
短文和问题都只播放一遍。

4
00:00:18,800 --> 00:00:27,040
After you hear a question, you must choose the best answer from the four choices, marked A, B, C and D.
听完问题后，你必须从标记为 A、B、C 和 D 的四个选项中选出最佳答案。

5
00:00:27,040 --> 00:00:33,220
Then Mark, the corresponding letter on answer sheet 1, with a single line through the center.
然后在答题卡 1 上相应的字母中心划一条单线进行涂黑。

6
00:00:34,660 --> 00:00:35,560
Passage 1.
短文 1。

7
00:00:36,440 --> 00:00:38,000
Talking is unique to humans.
说话是人类独有的。

8
00:00:38,640 --> 00:00:44,620
An animal might make ten different sounds, but an adult human knows more than 20,000 words.
动物可能会发出十种不同的声音，但成年人类掌握的词汇量超过 20,000 个。

9
00:00:45,200 --> 00:00:50,980
Additionally, we're the only animal that expresses thoughts in full sentences. Researchers
此外，我们是唯一能用完整的句子表达思想的动物。研究人员

10
00:00:50,980 --> 00:00:52,780
don't think language was invented.
并不认为语言是被发明出来的。

11
00:00:53,380 --> 00:00:55,420
Instead, they think it evolved.
相反，他们认为语言是进化而来的。

12
00:00:55,420 --> 00:00:57,580
How did talking evolve?
说话是如何进化的？

13
00:00:58,180 --> 00:00:59,760
There are two main theories.
主要有两种理论。

14
00:01:00,580 --> 00:01:06,360
The first theory is that language started with people making different sounds, mostly imitating
第一种理论认为，语言始于人们发出的各种声音，主要是模仿
 
15
00:01:06,360 --> 00:01:11,980
the things around them, like animal calls, nature sounds, and the sounds of tools.
周围的事物，如动物的叫声、自然界的声音以及工具发出的声音。

16
00:01:12,760 --> 00:01:17,640
Perhaps they made the sound of wind to comment on the weather, or imitated the sound
也许他们通过模拟风声来评论天气，或者模仿

17
00:01:17,640 --> 00:01:20,840
of a bird, to tell a friend that there was a bird nearby.
鸟叫声来告诉朋友附近有一只鸟。

18
00:01:20,840 --> 00:01:27,640
Then, over hundreds of thousands of years, those sounds turned into words that people began
然后，经过数十万年的演变，这些声音变成了人们开始

19
00:01:27,640 --> 00:01:29,720
to learn as part of their language.
学习并作为其语言一部分的单词。

20
00:01:30,320 --> 00:01:35,340
At some point, people started stringing the words together to form sentences.
在某个时间点，人们开始将单词串联起来组成句子。

21
00:01:36,480 --> 00:01:42,920
The other main theory, which is more recent, is that people started off by gesturing, pointing
另一种较新的主要理论认为，人们最初是通过打手势、

22
00:01:42,920 --> 00:01:47,240
at things with their hands, and imitating actions using their bodies.
用手指向物体以及用身体模仿动作开始交流的。

23
00:01:47,240 --> 00:01:52,000
Eventually, these gestures turned into a full sign language.
最终，这些手势演变成了一种完整的符号语言（手语）。

24
00:01:52,760 --> 00:01:58,440
This theory guesses that after developing sign languages, people eventually started
该理论推测，在发展出符号语言之后，人们最终开始

25
00:01:58,440 --> 00:02:01,000
making sounds along with their gestures.
伴随着手势发出声音。

26
00:02:01,740 --> 00:02:07,660
At some point, they switched to mostly making sounds that became words instead of just
在某个时刻，他们转而主要通过发出声音（即词汇）来交流，而不是仅仅

27
00:02:07,660 --> 00:02:08,780
using their bodies.
使用肢体。

28
00:02:09,460 --> 00:02:15,080
The reason they switched to making sounds, the theory goes, is that talking out loud
该理论认为，他们转向发声的原因在于，大声说话

29
00:02:15,080 --> 00:02:19,140
lets you communicate with someone even when you can't see them.
让你即使在看不见对方的情况下也能进行交流。

30
00:02:19,820 --> 00:02:24,220
Questions 16 to 18 are based on the passage you have just heard.
问题 16 至 18 基于你刚刚听到的短文。

31
00:02:25,040 --> 00:02:25,900
Question 16.
问题 16。

32
00:02:26,600 --> 00:02:30,040
